_comment: COUPLING tier-2. Verifies the sides-table claim that FEniCSx and scikit-fem each take EITHER side and were coupled to each other on this install with non-matching interface meshes. Runs three real couplings through the REGISTERED `couple` tool (fenics-Dirichlet/skfem-Neumann, skfem-Dirichlet/fenics-Neumann, fenics-Neumann/skfem-Dirichlet) at theta=1/(1+rho) and, for each, asserts against the CLOSED FORM of the split conduction problem: interface temperature, interface flux density on both sides with opposite signs, arclength-integrated flux balance, an empty `validation` block, and that the two sides really used different numbers of interface points. Convergence alone is deliberately NOT the assertion: a partitioned iteration converges to a fixed point, which is the solution only if the exchanged quantity, its sign and its units are all right — a unit mismatch converges and balances perfectly (see coupling/unit_mismatch_survives_every_internal_check). No number is pinned; the tolerances are what the physics must beat and the errors are printed.

_mutation.note: Configure both participants with a conductivity 25% away from the one the closed form is computed from. The coupling stays SELF-CONSISTENT: it converges, the two sides still agree at the interface, and the flux balance is untouched because both subdomains moved together — the interface temperature does not even change, since the conductance RATIO is preserved. Only the interface FLUX moves, by the same 25%. So this is a converged, balanced, internally unimpeachable coupling of the wrong problem, which is the exact silent-wrong shape these fixtures exist to catch, and the q_err check is the only thing that sees it. Run by hand against the subject rather than the setup, the equivalent was flipping the sign of `normal_fluxes` in data/coupling_participants/participant_skfem.py (not stageable, so not declarable here): that produced a run which converged in 62 iterations and balanced to 3.9e-08 while landing 22 K from the exact interface temperature.
